title: Collaborative Development Project
summary: A team of five or six first-years builds a client/server application in Java from a given product backlog, with a Spring Boot server and a JavaFX client. Six lectures in the first three weeks cover Git, build servers, teamwork, the technology stack, Scrum, requirements and accessibility; after that the course is almost entirely project work, with a weekly lab and a one-hour meeting with your TA. There is no exam: you are graded on what your team and you personally leave behind in GitLab.

basis.description: Slides of the six lectures, the 2024-25 assessment design document, the NetNote product backlog and the self-study sheets of CSE1105 Collaborative Software Engineering Project, the predecessor. Time shares count content slides; the opening organisation part of Lecture 1 is left out.
basis.caveat: CSE100 replaces CSE1105 from 2026-27 and moves from quarter 2 to quarter 4, so the schedule, the project (NetNote was the 2024-25 project) and its extensions will differ. Slide counts favour the image-heavy Teamwork and Accessibility lectures and understate Lecture 3, which packs dependency injection, Spring Boot, JavaFX and JSON into one slot.

topics.name: Git and version control
lectures: Lecture 1 - Organization & Project, Version Control & Build Basics
know: Working directory, staging area (index) and repository, and how add, reset, commit and checkout move changes between them
History as a graph of commits identified by SHA hashes; a branch is only a movable pointer to a commit
Trunk-based development versus feature branches, and why feature branches keep unfinished work out of main
Two-way versus three-way merge: knowing the common base version is what lets Git resolve most conflicts automatically
Remotes such as origin, remote-tracking branches, and the fetch, pull and push cycle
Which changes provoke conflicts: deleting or renaming files, changing method signatures, large refactorings
Line endings, SSH keys and a .gitignore that keeps target/, IDE folders and OS files out of the repository
do: Create a feature branch, commit, push it and merge it back through a GitLab merge request
Resolve a merge conflict by hand from the conflict markers Git writes into the file
Configure Git with your full name and TU Delft email so your contributions can be attributed to you
pitfalls: Committing under a different name or email than your merge commits use: the Git assignment checks this, and work under an unknown address is not credited to you
Integrating rarely: conflicting work then surfaces late, so commit early and merge main into your branch often
Squashing a feature branch into one commit: the staff then see only one commit, while you must commit several times every week

topics.name: Build automation, CI and code style
lectures: Lecture 1 - Organization & Project, Version Control & Build Basics
know: The steps of a build: resolve dependencies, compile, run unit tests, package, verify, deploy, report
Why manual builds fail: no reproducibility, no traceability, human error, and the it-works-on-my-machine problem
The build server as a neutral third party; GitLab pipelines and jobs, and where to read a failing build log
Maven and its pom.xml: project structure, plugins, main class and dependencies
The two team rules: a green main build has top priority, and whatever you value should be able to fail the build
Checkstyle, and the course requirement that each team picks at least 10 rules and enforces them in the build
do: Read a pipeline log and find why a build failed
Add a dependency or a Checkstyle rule to the Maven configuration
Keep the build of main green and the pipeline under about three minutes
pitfalls: Tests that exist but are not run by the build server count as poor in the testing rubric
Merging with a failing pipeline or leaving a broken build for more than a day lowers the build-server grade

topics.name: Teamwork: agreements, meetings and feedback
know: The code of conduct: topics it must cover (ambition, planning, communication, decisions, broken agreements, escalation) and why every agreement must be SMART
Three influence principles that make agreements stick: consensus (group norms), consistency (written, public, voluntary commitments) and liking
Meeting roles: the chair prepares the agenda and leads, the minute taker records decisions and actions, participants prepare too
Setting a purpose for each agenda item (inform, inventory, brainstorm, discuss, decide) and stating what, why and how
Content, process and relation as three levels present in every interaction, and frames of reference behind one-sided stories
Active listening, summarising, questioning and the use of silence; the risk of groupthink
The AID model for feedback: Action (an observed fact), Impact (its effect on you, from the I perspective), Desired change; feedback versus complaining
do: Write SMART team agreements with a clear procedure for when to involve the TA or lecturers
Prepare an agenda from the template with a time estimate for every item, and chair a meeting to it
Take minutes that end in an action list saying who does what by when
Write a Buddycheck tip in AID form and a top backed by an observable fact
pitfalls: Feedback that interprets or labels (you are sloppy) instead of describing a concrete, recent action fails the AID check
Writing the impact as the whole team being blocked or as blame; the rubric wants your own observed effect
Tops that praise a personal quality rather than a concrete performance fail
Leaving role rotation too late: everyone must have chaired and taken minutes at least once, and there are only about six TA meetings

topics.name: Dependency injection and testable design
know: The dependency inversion principle: high-level and low-level code both depend on an abstraction
Dependency injection: a component receives the components it depends on (DOCs) from outside instead of creating them
The strategy pattern as dependency inversion in action, and how a framework such as Guice wires the objects for you
Constructor injection (always valid, easy to test, long constructors) versus field injection (shorter, needs reflection, fields empty in the constructor); setter injection combines the drawbacks
Why static fields, static methods and hand-made singletons make code hard to use and hard to test
do: Refactor a class that creates its own dependencies into one that receives them
Write a test double for an interface and use it to test a class's input, output and call order
pitfalls: Calling new on a dependency inside a constructor or writing a singleton: the Technology rubric rates this poor or insufficient
Using static fields for anything other than constants

topics.name: Spring Boot server
know: Controllers with request mappings for GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, path variables, request parameters and request bodies
The Spring component model: @Component, @Controller and @RestController, @Service, @Repository, @Configuration with @Bean, and component scanning
Bean scopes (application, session, request) and why Spring manages component lifetimes for you
Persistence with JPA: @Entity classes, JpaRepository interfaces with custom queries, and the database console for inspection
Testing controllers and services as plain unit tests with injected test doubles
Debugging REST endpoints with Postman and a debugger attached to the server
do: Add a REST endpoint that takes a path variable or request body and returns a JSON object
Move logic out of a controller into a @Service and inject it
Store and query an entity through a Spring repository
Write a unit test for an endpoint
pitfalls: Mapping JSON to strings by hand in the server: Spring already does this with Jackson
Putting all logic in controllers; the top rubric level wants services, controllers and configuration kept apart

topics.name: JavaFX client and JSON object mapping
know: Stage, scene and the scene graph; building a UI in code versus in FXML with Scene Builder
Controllers, fx:id and FXML field injection, and implementing Initializable to finish set-up
The template project: Guice with MyFXML injects dependencies into controllers, and MainCtrl switches scenes to avoid cyclic dependencies between them
JSON types and why you design proper Java classes instead of thinking about the wire format
Object mapping with Jackson: ObjectMapper, a no-argument constructor for the mapper, equals and hashCode on shared classes
Calling the server from the client with the Jersey (JAX-RS) client in ServerUtils, with data classes shared through the commons module
do: Create a scene with a button and a label and switch between two scenes
Add a data class to commons and send it from client to server and back as JSON
Keep UI code, server communication and business logic in separate classes
pitfalls: Writing or parsing JSON yourself; the lectures call it wasted time and the rubric marks it poor
Mixing UI code with server requests; separating them is the step from sufficient to good in the client rubric

topics.name: Scrum and agile planning
lectures: Lecture 4 - Project Management and Requirements Engineering
know: The waterfall model and its limits, and the agile movement as the response
Scrum roles: Scrum Master, Product Owner, developers
Scrum artefacts and events: product backlog, sprint planning and sprint backlog, sprint, daily scrum, sprint review, retrospective
Estimating with story points and planning poker on a Fibonacci scale, and filling a sprint to the team's average velocity
Sprint boards with a shared definition of done, and burndown charts
Scrum as adapted for this course: a fixed backlog, one-week sprints, the TA meeting as review and planning, the retrospective among students only
do: Run a sprint review, retrospective and planning inside one TA meeting
Estimate tasks and choose next week's milestone from what the team actually achieved in earlier weeks
pitfalls: Filling a milestone with what must get done rather than what past weeks show you can do
Showing the TA features that are not merged into main: the demo must be potentially shippable

topics.name: Requirements engineering
lectures: Lecture 4 - Project Management and Requirements Engineering
know: Understanding the domain: the client's terminology, stakeholders and their conflicting needs
User requirements versus system requirements, and functional versus non-functional requirements (product, organisational, external)
User stories in the form as a role, I want something, so that some goal; epics, and acceptance criteria
Use cases with actor, preconditions, main scenario and alternate flows for failure cases
Requirements engineering as an incremental process: details emerge, mock-ups help, products are always underspecified
A user story is not a task: one story splits into several technical tasks of about one 3 to 4 hour work session
do: Break a user story from the backlog into concrete technical tasks (UI, data model, endpoint, validation, tests)
Write acceptance criteria for a story whose effect is ambiguous, and check them with your TA
pitfalls: Using backlog user stories directly as issues: the Tasks and Planning rubric rates this poor

topics.name: Accessibility and usability
know: Disability as a mismatch between a person and their environment, and physical, conceptual, economic, cultural and social exclusion

Seven universal design principles: use that is equitable and flexible, simple and intuitive operation, information every user can perceive, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and enough size and space for approach and use
Equal versus equitable treatment
Multiple modalities (text, colour, icon, shape, location), sufficient colour contrast and WCAG contrast levels AA and AAA
Good error messages: visible, saying what went wrong, why, and how to fix it; anticipating user errors and system errors such as an unreachable server
Fitts's law: target size and distance decide how quickly a target can be hit
Keyboard access, avoiding keyboard deadlocks, and information architecture (content, context, users)
do: Check an interface for contrast, keyboard-only navigation and multi-modal cues
Add keyboard shortcuts, confirmation dialogs for irreversible deletes, and informative feedback after actions
Implement multi-step undo with the command pattern
pitfalls: Not catching an exception at all, so the user cannot be told an error happened
Conveying status by colour alone instead of pairing it with text or an icon

topics.name: Merge requests, code review and GitLab issues
know: GitLab as a collaboration platform on top of Git: merge requests are a forge feature, not git merge or git pull
Why every change to main is reviewed: catching mistakes, knowledge transfer, quality and style checks
Developer rules: small, focused merge requests from up-to-date branches, one shared formatter, refactorings agreed with the team
Reviewer rules: look at meaning as well as syntax, a review is a conversation, review within two to three days, approve only what is ready
Draft merge requests, approvals reset by new commits, and not closing or merging someone else's merge request
Issues with a clear title, context, actions and acceptance criteria; assignees, labels, /estimate and /spend time tracking
Weekly milestones and boards, with coarse plans further out and finer ones close by
do: Open a merge request with a clear title and description and respond to review comments
Write review comments that suggest concrete improvements
Create, label, estimate and assign issues linked to their user story, and track time spent on them
pitfalls: Approving with a quick looks good to me while the pipeline is failing
Huge merge requests that tangle several tasks; they are slow to review and score low on reviewability
Checklists inside one issue instead of separate smaller issues

prerequisites: Object-oriented programming in Java at the level of the first-year programming course; the lecturers warn that you must catch up early if you are not there yet
Software testing and process basics from Software Design and Engineering, which runs in the quarter before
Basic HTTP: methods, requests and responses
A working set-up of Git, Maven, a recent JDK and JavaFX in an IDE before the first lab
practical: The whole course is one team project. In 2024-25 teams built NetNote, a note-taking app with a Spring Boot server and a JavaFX client sharing Jackson-mapped data classes, starting from a template project with client, server and commons modules. A set of basic requirements must work to pass; extensions (multiple collections, embedded files, links and tags, live sync over WebSockets, a language switch) raise the grade. Each week has a lab with a mandatory TA meeting that your team runs itself. Individually you do a Git assignment in week 1 and must keep contributing code, merge requests and reviews every project week.
studyAdvice: Do the Git assignment and the Spring, JavaFX and object-mapping self-studies in the first two weeks; the whole project rests on them, and the Git assignment is pass/fail.

Process carries more weight than features: tasks and planning plus code contribution and reviews are half the grade, features only a quarter. Set up issues, estimates, milestones and small merge requests from the first project week.

Plan for the weekly minimum from week 3 on: a finished merge request with Java code, about 100 lines of Java, one review comment of 100 or more characters and one approval. Two weak weeks in a row remove you from the course.
Take work by feature, not by layer, so you write both client and server code; the final check needs at least 100 lines on each side.
Finish every basic requirement first, then polish a few extensions to a high level; a complete extension earns more than several half-built ones.

Reread the accessibility checklist early: its nine criteria (contrast, shortcuts, keyboard flows, undo, error messages, feedback, delete confirmation) are cheaper to design in than to bolt on in week 9.
Use the formative feedback: it uses the same rubrics as the final grading, and grading looks mostly at the last weeks, so you can still recover.
